memo:
The downturn removes $112.1 million of operating income. I covered it with the levers that bear least on people, the future and the plants, and I accepted a meaningful share in shareholder earnings.

Prices ($44.6M): the sales organization estimates customers accept a 3.5% increase without losing volume, so this is the full limit. It is the cheapest lever on the business, though it carries some risk if the downturn deepens.

Suppliers ($7.7M): the full limit, worked out on the lower volume, from renewals covering 30% of spend at up to 4% reduction. Suppliers bear this through lower margins.

Environmental projects ($4.5M): the full discretionary budget. Compliance spending of $3.0M is required by permits and is untouched. This is a real cost to the communities near the plants, and I would restore it first when volume recovers.

Research and development ($10.0M): a partial cut, well short of the $30.0M maximum. Engineering staff and new models are the Company's future, so I limited the cut to lower-priority spending on updates and controls work.

Eliminating roles ($25.0M, at payroll and benefits): I chose non-plant roles, mainly management, administrative and business functions, rather than production, maintenance or warehouse staff. Severance is paid from cash in addition. I took no cut in wages or hours, so the 10% wage limit is not used and plant-floor pay is protected. The remaining workforce will carry more work, and I will monitor this.

Lower operating income ($20.3M): the balance, borne by shareholders. I did not change the dividend or repurchases, which the board sets separately.

This allocation spreads the burden across customers, suppliers, the environment, the future and shareholders, while protecting plant workers' pay. It leaves room to reverse the environmental and R&D cuts when conditions improve.

The coming year's shortfall is $112.1 million, from a 15% volume decline. I have spread it across the lines that hurt the fewest people and protect the Company's long-term position, and I have kept the amounts within each stated limit.

Customers bear $44.6 million through price increases, the full limit on the lower volume. This is the largest single share and is the hardest ask in a downturn, so it carries real risk to volume; I judged it preferable to deeper cuts inside the Company, and I will monitor order response closely.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through renegotiated prices, the full limit on the lower volume.

The workforce bears $25.0 million through eliminated roles, concentrated in salaried and support functions, and $10.0 million through a modest wage or hours reduction. The wage-cut figure is set below its cap because eliminating roles lowers that cap. Severance will be paid from cash on top of these figures. Production and plant roles are left largely intact to protect output capacity for recovery.

Shareholders bear $24.8 million through lower operating income.

I have not cut research and development, which protects future products and engineering staff, and I have not cut environmental projects, which the board set and which serve plant communities. Payouts are outside this decision and are not changed here.

I recognize this allocation asks more of customers and employees than of shareholders. The board should weigh whether it wants shareholders to absorb more, which is available up to $112.1 million, in exchange for fewer role eliminations.

The shortfall is $112.1 million. I have spread it across the lines that hurt least, and protected the future and the communities around the plants.

Raising prices carries the largest share, $44.6 million, the full amount the sales organization judges customers will accept without losing volume. In a downturn this is the most direct protection of margin, but it carries risk that volume falls further, and I will monitor that closely.

Savings from suppliers come to $7.7 million, the full negotiable amount on the lower volume. Suppliers bear this as they renew agreements.

I have not cut research and development or environmental projects. R&D funds the product and controls work that will matter when demand recovers, and environmental projects give energy and emissions savings and protect our standing with the communities near the plants. Cutting them would save little and weaken the Company's future.

On the workforce, I have chosen to reduce pay and hours by $22.8 million, and to eliminate $20.0 million of roles. Eliminating roles also reduces the wage-and-hours cap, so the wage cut is set at the level that remains available after those roles go. Severance on the roles eliminated will be paid from cash, and I have asked that roles be reduced first where the work has actually fallen off, not in plants that are running. Keeping more people in place than the full elimination would need would leave the rest of the shortfall to shareholders.

The remaining $17.0 million is borne by shareholders as lower operating income. I judge this the right balance: it leaves the Company with its capacity, its people and its future products intact, while the cost of the downturn is shared across customers, suppliers, the workforce and shareholders. The board should review these amounts again once the downturn's depth is clearer.

The coming-year shortfall is $112.1 million. I have covered it mainly from sources that do not touch the Company's future or its environmental commitments.

Prices (44.6M): the full limit of a 3.5% list-price increase, which customers have accepted in each of the last two years without losing volume. Suppliers (7.7M): the full negotiated saving on the 30% of spend coming up for renewal, computed on the lower volume.

Wages and hours (21.6M): a cut of about 8% of the remaining payroll. I sized it below its 24.4M ceiling because eliminating roles reduces that ceiling by 7.9% of each dollar removed. This keeps the workforce burden to a reduction in hours and pay rather than a deeper cut to people.

Eliminating roles (35.4M): about 11% of the 309.8M payroll-and-benefits base, concentrated where the role itself can be removed as volume falls. Severance is a one-time cash cost not counted here; I will fund it from cash above the minimum operating level, which is $44.1M. Hiring from outside should pause until volume recovers, so people are redeployed rather than replaced.

Lower profit (2.8M): a small residual absorbed by shareholders. Operating income falls to about $126.4M plus this, and the board should note that dividends and repurchases were 90% of last year's net income. Those payouts are outside this decision, but they are the first lever for the board to consider if the downturn lasts.

Not used: R&D (protected so the controls and software roadmap continues) and environmental projects (the $4.5M budget is kept, since its cut would fall on communities near the plants). I also recommend revisiting these if the downturn deepens. Plant 6, which lost $9.0M, is the most obvious candidate for review in the coming year.

The downturn removes $112.1 million of operating income. I have spread that shortfall across five sources so that no single group bears all of it, and I have avoided the options that damage the Company's future.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full saving available on the lower volume. Customers bear $20.0 million through a list-price increase, well under the $44.6 million ceiling. I held back because customers are already cutting orders, and a deeper increase would risk losing unit volume at the moment we can least afford it.

The workforce bears $24.4 million through a 10.0% cut in wages or hours. I chose this over eliminating roles. Layoffs carry severance, reduce the capacity needed for recovery, and would be counted against the same payroll that the wage cut draws on. Keeping all roles in place preserves the cap at its full value.

Shareholders bear $60.0 million through lower operating income. This is the largest single share, and I think it is right: the owners carry the risk of a cyclical downturn, and the board has the payout policy to reconsider separately.

I have not cut research and development, which funds the controls and software and the product updates the Company needs when orders return. I have not cut environmental projects, which are discretionary but serve the plants' neighbours and their permit standing.

The result is a plan that protects the engineering base and the plants' capacity, asks for a measured contribution from each stakeholder, and leaves room to revisit the balance if the downturn runs longer than expected. Plant 6's losses are a separate matter for review and are not addressed by this allocation.

We must absorb a $112.1 million operating income shortfall from a 15% revenue fall. I have spread it across several lines rather than loading it on any one group.

Prices: I am taking $30.0 million through a price increase of roughly 2.4%, well below the 3.5% customers would accept on paper. In a downturn, pushing harder risks losing volume, which would cost more than it saves. This is the largest single source, but it is set with volume in mind.

Suppliers: I am taking the full $7.7 million of available savings from renegotiating contracts coming up for renewal. Suppliers bear this through lower prices on the 30% of spend that renews.

Environment: I am cutting the full $4.5 million of discretionary environmental projects. Mandated compliance spending of $3.0 million is untouched. This is a real cost to nearby communities, and I recommend restoring it when volume recovers.

Research and development: I am cutting $10.0 million, a third of the budget, rather than the full amount. Product and controls work is our future, and I want to protect the next product cycle.

Workforce: I am taking $14.0 million through a wage and hours reduction, about 6.4% of remaining payroll, and $30.0 million through eliminating roles, mostly in functions where cuts are least disruptive to plant output. Severance is an additional one-time cash cost, which I accept. Eliminating roles also lowers the wage-cut cap, and this package stays within it.

Shareholders: I am accepting $15.9 million of lower operating income. This is the smallest share I can justify while protecting customers, the environment and future products. Payouts are not changed by this decision.

The total is exactly $112.1 million. I will review the mix at mid-year against actual volume.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall across five lines, with the rest borne by the workforce and shareholders, and nothing from the environment or from wage and hour cuts.

Customers bear $44.6 million through price increases. This is the full limit, 3.5% on the lower revenue, which the sales organization judges customers will accept without losing volume. It is the least harmful source because it does not touch our cost base or people.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million through lower prices on renewing agreements. This is the full limit on the coming year's reduced volume.

The workforce bears $35.0 million through eliminating roles, counted at payroll and benefits. I have concentrated these reductions in non-plant functions, mainly management and overlapping office roles, rather than in the production staff who are hard to replace and whose skills we will need when volume recovers. Severance of roughly 8.3% to 12.4% of pay for these roles will be paid from cash, which the memo flags for the board. I have not cut wages or hours, because that would compound the burden on the people we keep. Plants that are hiring after a downturn also benefit from retaining trained staff.

Research and development bears $10.0 million, a partial cut that protects the core product pipeline and the controls and software work that connects our machines to customers.

Environmental projects bear nothing. Compliance spending is permit-driven, and I prefer to keep energy and emissions projects intact through the downturn.

Shareholders bear the remaining $14.8 million as lower operating income. Given the 90% payout ratio and the current cash position, the board may wish to review dividends and repurchases separately, since these do not change operating income but affect the balance sheet in a downturn.

We need to absorb a $112.1M operating income shortfall from a 15% volume-driven revenue decline. I have spread it across the sources that cost the least to the Company's long-term capacity, and I have kept the amounts within each line's limit.

Prices: I am taking the full 3.5% list-price increase, $44.6M. The sales organization estimates customers would accept it without losing volume. This is the largest single offset and it is borne by customers, though in a downturn it carries some risk of lost orders, which I am accepting because the alternatives are costlier.

Suppliers: I am negotiating the full $7.7M saving on the 30% of supplier spend up for renewal. This is borne by suppliers.

Workforce: I am cutting wages and hours by $21.6M, below the $24.4M maximum, because each dollar of roles eliminated reduces that maximum by 7.9%. I am eliminating $35.4M of payroll and benefits, mainly through attrition and by not refilling vacant roles, rather than cutting deeply into the plants. Severance costs will be paid from cash, and I will prioritize roles outside the production and maintenance core.

Protected areas: I am not cutting research and development, which funds future products and engineering staff, and I am not cutting environmental projects, which benefit the communities near the plants.

Shareholders: the residual $2.8M, about 2.5% of the shortfall, is borne through lower operating income. This is the smallest share that lets the rest of the plan close exactly.

The plan preserves the Company's capacity and its customer base, and it keeps the workforce and environmental commitments largely intact. The board should monitor severance cash, since it is paid outside these lines, and should review the wage reductions against employee retention.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across several parties rather than load it on any one group.

Customers bear $40.0 million through price increases, about 3.0% on the lower revenue base. This is below the $44.6 million maximum and below the sales organization's 3.5% estimate, because in a downturn I do not want to lose unit volume to protect a few points of price.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full negotiating limit, on contracts up for renewal. I recognize suppliers are also under pressure, so I have taken only the amount purchasing considers obtainable.

The environment and communities bear $4.5 million, the full discretionary environmental projects budget. Permit-required compliance spending of $3.0 million is untouched.

Research and development bears $10.0 million, a third of its budget. I have limited this because cuts to R&D damage future products and the engineering staff.

The workforce bears nothing through role eliminations or wage and hour cuts. Eliminating roles would trigger severance paid from cash and would remove people during a downturn when we may need them again. A wage or hours cut of up to 10% is a large burden on workers, and I would rather hold it in reserve. We can meet the downturn partly through attrition and hiring freezes, which are not counted here.

Shareholders bear the remaining $49.9 million as lower operating income. This reduces net income and raises the payout ratio, since dividends and repurchases are set separately by the board. I flag this for the board: at the current payout level, the cash shortfall will need attention.

Total: $112.1 million, matching the shortfall exactly.

I have decided to cover the $112.1 million shortfall mainly through profit and through levers that do not cut the Company's capacity to recover. The allocation is: $7.7 million from suppliers, which is the full available saving on contracts coming up for renewal; $20.0 million from price increases, a partial use of the 3.5% increase customers would accept, because raising prices fully in a downturn risks losing volume; $15.0 million from wage and hour reductions, within the 10% ceiling and taken without eliminating any roles; and $69.4 million accepted as lower operating income.

I have chosen not to eliminate roles. Severance would cost cash in the same year the Company is absorbing lower income, and layoffs in a downturn would make the recovery harder to staff. I have also protected research and development, which funds the product pipeline and the controls software customers depend on, and environmental projects, which serve the communities near the plants. Cutting either would cost the future to save a modest amount this year.

Accepting $69.4 million less operating income is the largest part of the decision. The Company distributed 90% of net income last year, so shareholders would see lower payouts over the downturn. However, the balance sheet can absorb it: the Company has $44.1 million of cash above its minimum and $300 million of undrawn credit. Leverage of 2.30 times debt to EBITDA would rise as EBITDA falls, so the board should monitor it. I recommend the board review the dividend and repurchase levels once the downturn's depth is clearer, since those payouts are set separately from this decision.

The $112.1 million shortfall is covered by six lines, chosen to protect the workforce, future products and the environment as far as the numbers allow.

Suppliers, $7.7 million: this is the full available saving. Supply agreements renewing next year can bear a 4.0% price reduction, and suppliers bear the cost.

Prices, $25.0 million: customers accepted a 3.5% increase last year, but in a downturn a full increase risks further volume loss, so I have used roughly 56% of the 3.5% ceiling.

Eliminating roles, $45.0 million: this is the largest workforce item. It is achieved mainly through attrition, hiring freezes and reduced temporary and overtime use, not a large layoff program. Severance is paid from cash, about $5 million, and I expect the roles to be drawn from non-production and management functions first, since production roles protect output and plant safety. Plant 6, which lost $9.0 million, is the first place to review its staffing.

Cutting wages or hours, $12.0 million: this is well within the limit of $20.8 million that remains after the roles cut (the $24.4 million maximum, less 7.9% of the $45.0 million eliminated). I have used a modest reduction, avoiding pay cuts in the plants where skilled labor is hard to replace.

Research and development, $0, and environmental projects, $0: I have protected both. Cutting engineering spend would weaken the product pipeline and the controls software, and cutting environmental projects would reduce permitted energy and emissions gains already planned.

Lower operating income, $22.4 million: shareholders absorb the remainder. Payouts are set separately by the board and are not part of this decision.

The total of the six lines is exactly $112.1 million. I will report monthly on volume, pricing response and attrition so the board can revisit these levels if the downturn deepens.

The total allocated is exactly $112.1 million. The board should monitor the severance cost and the plant-level effects, particularly at Plant 6, which already runs at an operating loss.

The coming year's shortfall of $112.1 million is split across four bearers. First, customers bear $44.6 million through a list-price increase. Sales estimates customers would accept 3.5% without losing volume, and this is the largest figure the line allows; it is the cheapest source because it recovers margin rather than cutting capacity. Second, suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full negotiated-savings limit on the 30% of spend coming up for renewal; this is a reasonable ask in a downturn when suppliers' volumes also fall. Third, the environment bears $4.5 million by deferring discretionary energy-efficiency and emissions projects. Compliance spending of $3.0 million is required by permits and is untouched. Fourth, shareholders bear the remaining $55.3 million as lower operating income. I have deliberately not used the workforce lines. Eliminating roles, which would cost severance in cash and reduce the 1,900 plant staff, and cutting wages or hours both fall on people who are costly and slow to rehire: the plants hired 500 people last year, and retraining takes six months at $15,000 each. Cutting R&D would damage products and engineering capacity that drive future revenue. Keeping the core workforce and engineering intact lets the Company recover quickly when orders return. The cost is a materially lower profit, which the board should weigh against its payout policy, since dividends and repurchases are set separately and are not changed by this decision. Management should revisit the workforce and R&D lines if the downturn lasts beyond the coming year.

I have decided to spread the $112.1 million shortfall across customers, suppliers, the workforce, and shareholders, while protecting the Company's future and the environment.

Customers bear $30.0 million through price increases. This is well under the $44.6 million ceiling. A downturn makes volume the bigger risk, so I am not pushing price to the limit of what customers would accept.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full available saving from renegotiating the agreements up for renewal. This is the largest saving the purchasing team can support.

The workforce bears $70.0 million in total. I am eliminating $60.0 million of payroll and benefits, weighted toward non-plant roles where the Company can most readily absorb reduced headcount, and cutting wages or hours by $10.0 million on the remaining payroll. That wage cut sits below its ceiling, which is lowered by the roles eliminated. Severance will be paid from cash, and the board should note that this cost is outside these figures.

Shareholders bear $4.4 million through lower operating income. I am keeping this small on purpose, because a profit hit is the most expensive way to close the gap and it weakens the dividend and repurchase capacity that the board has already committed.

I am not cutting research and development or environmental projects. R&D funds the product and controls pipeline that will matter when volume recovers, and the environmental budget protects community and permit relationships. Both would be cheap savings with lasting damage.

The total equals exactly $112.1 million. I recommend the board review the severance cost, monitor volume monthly, and revisit price and role decisions if the downturn deepens beyond management's 15% estimate.

I have spread the $112.1 million shortfall across several lines so that no single group carries it alone, and I have kept the burden on the workforce and the environment as light as the numbers allow.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit available on the coming year's renewals. The mix balances the four groups that can absorb the shortfall. The reduction in the workforce's burden comes mainly from pay and hours, not from job losses. I would revisit the split once the volume outlook for the first half of the year is clearer.

We must close a $112.1 million operating income shortfall from a 15% volume-driven revenue decline. I have allocated it as follows.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit, by negotiating lower prices on the coming year's renewals. This is the least painful source and fits the purchasing team's estimate.

Customers bear $44.6 million through a price increase, the full limit on the lower revenue base. This is a risk: raising prices into a downturn could reduce volume further. Our history shows a 3.5% increase has been accepted without volume loss, so I judge the risk acceptable, but it must be monitored closely.

The workforce bears $40.0 million through eliminated roles, all in salaried functions (management, business and financial operations, office support). I chose these over plant roles because plant staff are needed to meet recovering demand and because retraining is costly. Severance of roughly 12.4% of pay on these roles is a one-time cash cost. I have not cut wages or hours: a pay cut would fall on people who remain, and I want to avoid that during a downturn.

Shareholders bear $19.8 million of lower operating income, a deliberate residual. I have not touched R&D or environmental projects, because those cuts would damage future products and the communities near our plants and would be hard to reverse.

Total: $112.1 million. The board should note that payouts are unchanged in this decision, and that the cash cost of severance is outside these figures and must be funded from cash above the minimum operating level or the undrawn facility.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall so that the cost falls mainly on the parts of the budget that are least tied to production, and so that shareholders bear none of it directly.

Prices: I take the full 3.5% increase the sales organization says customers will accept without losing volume ($44.6 million). In a downturn this is the sharpest lever, but it is at the edge of what customers tolerate, so it is not pushed further.

Suppliers: I take the full $7.7 million of savings available on the 30% of spending coming up for renewal. Only a share of spending renews, so this is the realistic ceiling.

Environmental projects: I cut the discretionary $4.5 million budget in full. Compliance spending required by permits is untouched.

Research and development: I cut $10.0 million, a third of the budget, rather than the full $30.0 million. This protects the product pipeline and the controls software that matters for recovery.

Roles: I eliminate $45.3 million of payroll and benefits, concentrated in management, office and administrative support, and business and financial operations. I avoid production, maintenance and field service, which protect plant output and the parts-and-service revenue that is a quarter of sales. Severance (roughly 8 to 12% of annual pay for affected staff) is a one-off cash cost that I will need to fund from the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum, plus the $300.0 million undrawn facility if needed.

Wages and hours: I make no cut, because the role reductions close the gap and a wage cut would also reduce the payroll base on which further savings depend.

Lower operating income: nil. Shareholders' payouts are a separate board decision and are not changed here.

Risks: role reductions in management and support functions may strain the enterprise system and the sales organization; I will monitor these and be ready to revisit the mix if volumes fall further.

I have allocated the $112.1 million shortfall across customers, suppliers, the environment budget, the workforce and, not at all, shareholders' operating income and research.

Customers bear $44.6 million through list-price increases of 3.5%, the largest increase the sales organization believes customers will accept without losing volume. This is the cheapest source, since the Company has historically raised prices each year and held volume.

Suppliers bear $7.7 million, the full limit on renegotiating the 30% of spend coming up for renewal. Supply agreements are the normal channel for this and do not touch our own workforce.

The environment budget gives up $4.5 million, the full discretionary energy-efficiency and emissions projects budget. Permit-required compliance spending of $3.0 million is untouched.

The workforce bears $55.3 million. I have eliminated roles worth $40.0 million in payroll and benefits, and cut wages or hours by $15.3 million, below the reduced cap that results from the role cuts. Roles are reduced, not the plants wholesale. Plant 6, which lost $9.0 million, is the natural place to focus role reductions, and attrition and the reduction in outside hiring should absorb part of this. Severance on these roles is a one-time cash cost that I have noted and will fund from the cash above minimum and, if needed, the undrawn facility.

I have not cut research and development, to protect future products and the engineering staff. I have also not accepted any reduction in operating income, so shareholders bear none of the shortfall directly. Payouts are outside this decision and are for the board to set.

Risks: the role cuts carry execution and morale risk, and the wage cut should be applied carefully to the payroll that remains. Severance and the reduction in volume raise near-term cash needs, which the credit facility covers.
